number, are best for the bodily well-being of
the worker, or for the advantage of the
capitalist. We are left entirely in the dark
as to whether we shall gain or lose as an in-
dustrial people by limiting or extending the
time we give to leisure and enjoyment of life,
or to the wearying drudgery whereby so many
are compelled to seek the means of living.

In the absence of this information the work-
ing people have undertaken to act for them-
selves. From the highest skilled artisans
down to the poor labourers in our fields,
including our seamstresses and domestic ser-
vants, a general, and Bo far successful, stand
has been made against long hours. When
the fight commenced, Sir WILLIAM ARMSTRONG
stood in the front, and fought stoutly against
short time, and it will not be forgotten that, as
the representative of capital, he endeavoured
to win the battle by the aid of foreign work-
men. To use a common phrase, "no stone
was left unturned" to defeat the English
workers on their own ground; but their resolu-
tion and union rendered the attempt abortive,
and secured for our men the limitation sought
for. From that moment the cause has pro-
gressed with accelerated speed. From thence-
forth nine hours will be reckoned as the
English working man's day, until, by the
progress of mechanical invention and the
additional power acquired thereby in produc-
tion, a further reduction of hours will seem
as reasonable, and in reality be as reasonable,
as that which is now taking place.

But a question of some importance arises
hero in regard to short time. We know what
Sir Witt. ARMSTRONG did as an employer of
labour, and we are pretty well acquainted with
what other large employers have done, The
very largest employer of labour in the
kingdom, however—the Government—has yet
to be brought to amount, that we may find out
how the many thousands working under it for
the country have been treated in this matter
of short time. The meeting last Saturday on
Plumstead Common was a significant fad. It
was a gathering exclusively composed of
workers in the Woolwich Arsenal, and its
purpose was to memorialise the Government for
the same conditions of work, as to time, which
have been introduced into private establish-
ments where a like kind of labour is carried
on. Nothing could be more respeotful or
temperate than the memorial adopted by those
assembled. There are many reasons why the
Government should comply with the request it
contains, and order their Centrollor-in-Chief
to at once set the question at rest by a ready
and frank compliance with the men's wishes.
This may be urged for several reasons which
ought to be considered as valid by Mr. GLAD-
STONE and his colleagues. Whether justly so
or not, they have lost ground amongst large
numbers of the working people by their treat-
ment of the dockyard labourers. In fact, for
many reasons, they are under suspicion, not
perhaps of unfriendliness to the claims of work-
ing men, but rather of abandoning those
olaims in deference to the interests of the
manufacturing and trading classes. To grant
what the men at Woolwich are now looking
for could not be regarded as a hid for the
working men's votes throughout the country,
simply because this would not be leading, but
following the lead of other employers. Such

mate, as sooner or later it must come; and it

THOSE who are anxious to know where the
present short time may make itself felt, or
where it will stop, will have, we apprehend,
to wait some time yet before their curiosity can
be gratified. The rapidity with which the differ-
ent classes of workers have followed each other
is proof of the state of preparedness amongst
.the masses of the people; whilst the general
public acquiescence with which their demands
have been received, is satisfaotory evidence of
their reasonableness. It is a curious fact that
no writer in the newspaper press or elsewhere
has attempted to define, oven in a loose way,
what the limits of, a day's work should be.
Neither on grounds of health nor on industrial
or economic grounds, has any expert under-
taken to inform the public whether five hours

would certainly be wiser for the present
Government to improve its position by timely
concession than leave it to their rivals and.
probable successors as a trump card to be
played when the exigency of the political
situation required it.
It is not to be believed that the men in the
Arsenal can be made exceptional subjects for
harsh treatment. Whatever has been ob-
tained by other men working at the same
trades for private employers will have to be
conceded to them, whether the Government
be Liberal or Conservative; and, therefore, our
present officials now possess the opportunity of
winning public favour by a necessary act of
justice; if they are wise they will not let it
slip. It is difficult to say how far the con-
duct of the Government may be influenced by
the keen parsimony of Mr. LOWE. It is pretty
well understood how anxious he i to get as
much as he can and give as little as possible—
especially if the intended recipients
are working men, and, above all, if
they are working men of the trades' union
kind, Ibr whom he has a very strong
dislike. But our Liberal rulers must not
forget that the great deciding power at our
parliamentary elections will henceforth rest
in the hands of working men. And they
must also bear in mind that the cause of
labour is now, in many ways, a matter of
public concernment. -Nothing in these days
of cheap newspapers is local. Everything
that concerns the well-being of any class or
section of the community is by our mans of
publicity made the subject of national discus-
sion. The demands of the artizans of the
Arsenal cannot, therefore, be shut up in Wool-
wioh or talked about only on Plumstead Com-
mon.

Their cause is the cause of labour everywhere
throughout Great Britain; and the workers of
other localities will most assuredly demand by
public remonstrance and protest that the
same rights they have won for themselves
shall be accorded to their fallow-men em-
ployed in the various Governments works.
It is very much to be desired that our
Liberal Ministry should not force on the work-
ing men of England the necessity of making
this question matter of public complaint, or of
exciting agitation. They have already lost
much of the public confidence by paltry
tinkerings, whore a frank and courageous
policy would have suited better. There never
was an Administration which suffered so much
by petty blundering, and if resistance to short
time as employers be added to their other sins,
they will be likely enough to produce a convic-
tion in the public mind that nothing can save
them from that self-destruotion towards which
they seem to be wilfully hurrying.
If Mr. GLA.DSIONE, and those around him
and under him as officials, would reflect on this
short-time movement amongst the masses of
the people, they would discover that it is not an
accident, not a whim, put into their minds by
an exceptional prosperity of trade, but a
settled policy, springing from two convictions,
which have for years been growing into shape
and rooting themselves firmly in working
men's minds. The present movement is, as it
were the first, strong wave of an inflowing
tide, and it will be well if those who hold
sway in the land, anci whose bu,4iness it is to
understand the actual life of the country,
regard it in connection with the living energy
by which it has beau thrown forward,

THE NEW CRIMINAL LAW AMEND-
MENT ACT.

Tan Bill of last year, which the Govern-
ment so shamefully mismanaged, has produced
in practice the evils which called out so many
protests. After bringing in A Bill framed on
unjust prinoiplee,, the Ministry saw its own
injustice exaggerated by the rancour of the
Peers, and isuffered a measure to pass which
they, themselves denounced. It was Mr.
11BA7C; 1111;013elf who said that under the new
Act a man standing at a factory door might be
convicted under. it. Nevertheless, Mr. BRUCE
permitted it to become law. His protest has
been abundantly justified, and men have been
imprisoned, for no greater offence than standing
at a factory doer.
The working of the new Act has entirely
borne out all our predictions. Men have been
arrested and imprisoned and in some cases
sentenced on the most frivolous pretences, so
frivolous that in several instances the prosecu-
tion bas been ultimately abandoned. And
althoUgh courts of appeal have not sanctioned
these proceedings, the evil has been done, long
before a court of appeal was reached. Violent
altercations and recriminations have arisen
amongst magistrates on the bench; trade
disputes have been embittered by oppressive
arrests; large sums have been taken from
working men in costs; and respectable men
have been outraged by prisons. Now this is
exactly what we predicted. Our objection to
the statute even more than to its actual
enactments was that it exceptionally entrusted
to a partizan magistracy the working out of a
very complicated penal legislation. We pro-
tested against the new law on the ground that
it was vague and exceptional; it made acts of
Workmen criminal, whilst leaving untouched
the corresponding acts of capitalists; and
lastly it put an exceptional power into the
hands of the prejudiced magistrate.
- The evils of this Act have led to atteraptt
to repeal it, or to modify it, and there is now
before the House a Bill by Mr. VERNON
HARCOURT and others to effect this object.
Whatever may be the history of this Bill, I
must at once pronounce it wholly insufficient
and illusory. Its promoters, no doubt, have
satisfied themselves that this is all that can be
asked of the present House. I will not enter
into that question; nor do I throw any doubt
on the public spirit and prudence of those
politicians who promote the Bill. It is
obviously, from their point of view, well

intended. But I emphatically protest against
this Bill being considered in any sense a solu-
tion of the question, and I warn working men
not to give it the smallest countenance. I
know not what show of .support the Bill may
have from working men's representatives; but
I know that the workmen as a body cannot
assent to anything of the kind. If it were
supposed that they had promoted this Bill?
their long opposition to the Combination Laws
and to the Act of last year would be
entirely stultified. The now Bill re-imposes
and repeats every one of the obnoxious
features of the Act of 1871, with the single
exception,that it omits the penalty on " watch-
ing and besetting." Now, I am quite aware
that this latter clause is the one most obviously
unjust in the late Act, but it was far from
being its only evil. The formal protest against
that Act signed by representative workmen,
and by the lawyers whom they had consulted,
condemned the Ad on many other grounds.
They protested against the vagueness of its
language, against the artificial nature of the
crimes it constituted, against its non-definition
of the word coerce, and against the unjust
nature of the tribunal it gave power to. The
new Bill repeats and re-enacts all these
features in the same language. But it does
more. For the first time it introduces a
penalty for a new crime, described in the
vaguest and most treacherous language. Even
the House of Lords, in its desire for new
penalties last year, did not venture to insert
such a clause as this which includes under
molestations "acts calculated to intimidate."
This loose and dangerous phrase is found for
the first time in the new Bill. So that this
new amendment is to reinforce in the old
words all the obnoxious features of the
last Act, leaving out "watching and be-
setting," but adding as a new charge "acts
calculated to intimidate."

I will only add that, whatever motives may
exist within the House of Commons for pro-
moting such a Bill, the workmen can have no
motive in countenancing it. It is distinctly
opposed to the formal protest of last year, and
to the condemnation of the Act passed. at the
Nottingham conference. And it has not had
the sanction of those who have advised. the
workmen in the matter. If the House of
Commons desires to pass the Bill, let them look
to it themselves, Working men and their
representatives can give this measure no
countenance, without being false to all that
they have hitherto argued, and to the true
interests of free labour.

AMALGAMATE'? SOCIETY OF RAILWAY

SERVANTS.

Iwisif to avail myielf of the opportunity of
laying before the railway servants throughout
the kingdom the present position of the affairs
of this Society, -so aa to prevent any mistakes,
and to conserve and consolidate such power as
can be obtained by united action.
It will be remembered that in Maroh last
a discussion was going on between the men in
the previnoes' and some of their brethren in
the metropolis, the ground of dispute being
whether or not the London men had been
justified in preparing rules and enrolling them,
and meeting certain officers. A. meeting took
place at the house of Mr. W. Miss, and it was
then suggested that the matters in difference
should be arranged at a conference of pro-
vincial representatives ana the London
Executive Council. That conference took
pint! on Saturday, April 20th, when twelve
members of the Council and twelve delegates
from the provinces were accepted as a com-
petent body to settle the differences and to
arrange for a delegate meeting at which all
parts of the country should be represented.
The programme of that delegate meeting
has been already published in your columns,
and it provides, amongst other things-1. That
the minority will accept the decision of the
majority, or in other words, that those who
May not carry any particular motion shall not
take -offlince thereat and recede 2. That for
tlie interval between that meeting and
the 24th of June Ur, JortN GitiliA:ll, Of

Derby, should act as temporary Geneial
Secretary for such of the provincial branches
as think fit to communicate with him; and

that Mr. GEORGE CHIPMAN shall act as
General Secretary for such of the metropolitan

members as think fit to communicate with

him; but that the Exeetative.Cuuneil shall be

_ .
accepted as the governing body until, after
the delegate meeting in June. By this course

it was in-tended, as-far as possible, to secure

the óo-operation of all, 'and to concentrate our
forces by complete union. Many exoellent
friends had been working in the dttue, but
their labours were comparatively useless
because the branches they formed, were not
affiliated with the Executive Council, or with
any central body. The motives of these
friends are not impugned, but their discretion
is, I think, open to . doubt, bemuse it' the
branches of a. tree are separate , from the
trunk they wither and die; and, it appears
to me'that it is of no use to rouse the men to
a sense of their wrongs if you do not; at the
same time, create add strengthen that union
Which 'alone can remedrthose wrongs.

The programme provided further for the
number of delegates to be sent bY a given
number of menibers, And for the business to
be done at, the delegate meeting. Arrange-
ments were also made for a public meeting of
railway servants and others oa the 27th of
June, beiug the last day of the Conference.
As one of the subjects which had excited a
good deal of feeling was the appointment of
the General Secretary, it was decided unani-
mously by the provincial and metropolitan
Men thus assembled that the appointifient
should be advertised, and a handsome salary
offered to any gentleman competent to under-
take the important and somewhat difficult
duties of the office. That advertisement was
published in the Times of Monday, lqay 20th,
and within 48 hours upwards of forty applica-
tions had been received from men of high
social rank, cerumeroial experience, univer-
sity acquirements, and public reputation. As
the intention to advertise had been made
known to all the branches by the pablioation
of the programme adopted at the preliminary
conference, it NVItS assumed that all those who
wet° counected with the meeem sett, who
intended to become candidates, would have
prepared to send in their applications, and.five
days were
,considered sufficient time within
which applications should be received. Before
the advertisement was published, it
was submitted to representative men in town
and country, and alterations made in accordance
with then. suggestions. The advertisement
stated that no application could be received
after the 24th Ma 3, and the list was them fore
closed on that day, and the Committee of
Selection are now buay in making a seleotion
Of six from. such applications in accordance
with the decision of the preliminary confer-
ence. Their task will be one of enormous
difficulty as wall as of tedious labour, as the
applications are about fifty or sixty in number.
The six names so selected are to be put to
the vote of the members by lists sent to each
braneh contributing its levy to the delegate
expense fund. I should have preferred the
preferential system of voting, and recom-
mended it to the provincial men through Mr.
GaiELIM, but his correspondents seem to prefer
the ordinary system of majority voting. Pro-
bably the plea ultimately decided upon will be
for the officers of each branch to give the
numbers of votes of their members for each
candidate (if there be any difference of opinion),
the names of the candidates nominated by the
selecting committee being placed in alpha-
betical order. I shall be glad to receive im-
mediate advise and. information from any
friends sufficiently interested to communicate
with me upon the subject. I trust that the
Committee of Seleetion will have made their
report on the six most suitable applications
before the 10th of June, and that the lists
will be sent out to all the branches who are
reported through Mr. CHIPAL&N or Mr. GRAllar
at that date, as provided by claire 10 of the
hecepted programme. Whatever names are
submitted by the Committee, I trust that the
men throughout the country will regard the
election as one of the deepest consequence to
themselves, and to the future of their class;
and that they will cast aide all personal con-

didations of every kiiiaiand dotal; &Teat
and best man.that can be obtitined.i
I do not ask the railway men to forget per-
sonal Bodices rendered to them by men who
are known and deservedly respected by them;
I ask them to estimate their services as they
severally deserve, and to show a grateful
liberality to theca each and all. The appoint-
ment of General Seeretary, however, may not
be a suitable reward for such labours. ; on the
eontrary, no greater cruelty could be inflicted
upon such friends than to place them in a
position which they may not be competent to
fill. I do. not presume to say that they are
incompetent, but whilst I estimate the good
qualities and the noble intentions of them all,

I notice an immense difference between the
fitness of some for an office where punctuality,
energy, untiring diligence, patient work,
prompt correspondence, financial accuracy,
and conscientious prudence, will be tasked to
the uttermost. I cannot advise that we
look amongst entire strangers, but rather
that we secure some one who has al-
ready given public guarantees of his
earnestness and ability. I have no
friend to recommend, and. 'no enemy to
oppose; I trust that the best man may win.
I have no personal interests to serve, because
fortunately I have no requirement for any
position which the Society could offer to me,
and the adviee I presume to give is that of a
man who only holds his official position as a

temporary arrangement until the permanent
constitution of the Society can be established
by the delegates and representatives of the
railway men themselves. My resignation will
be the first business of the meeting on the
24th of June. I shall then, I hope, feel that
my labours have been, to some extent, instru-
mental in consolidating union and removing
causes of dissension, and that my work is
done. Unless there are difficulties which,
after that time, call for my help, I see no
reason why I should sacrifice my comfort to
take part in an organization where, however
disinterestedly I may hint*, my motives and
my acts are wilfully misrepresented by a
newspaper, the mendacity and ignorance of
whose editor is a standing danger to the
mweinent,
.in which many earnest luau, are
engaged—a danger all the greater because the
enemy is hidden behind the mask of a hypo-
critical friend. To me personally his action
is beneath:contempt, but my time is too
valuable to myself to waste it in perpetual
explanations of the stupid errors, or in con-
tradictions of the still more stupid misrepre-
presentations of the person referred to. If the
railway men are to have an organ, they have
a right to insist that it shall be at least just to
their friends, or that it shall cease to be their
organ. If they cannot control it for good, the
sooner they take away from it that support
which enables it to be mischievous, the better.
• J. BAXTER LAYGLEY.

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.
I OBSERVE in the BEE-HIVE of May 25th
that, at a meeting held a few days ago, in
Herefordshire, in connection with the agricul-
tural labourers' movement, it was announced
by one of the speakers, Mr. GIBSON WARD,
that I bad consented to address a series of
meetings in that county. You will oblige me
by stating that his announcement is quite
incorrect, as I have neither consented, nor,
indeed, even been asked, to address a series of
such meetings.
EMIOND FITZUALTRICE.

THE PRESENT AND FUTURE RELA-
TION OF CAPITAL AND LABOUR.

• How long is the present senseless relation
between capital and• labour to continue? Yes
how long, asks common sense, are these vital
elements to the production of the necessities of
our life to be pitted against each other in deadly
hate, alike destructive to both? Talk of war!
What war can be more terrible, more destruc-
tive to our national physical well-being, more
withering to our moral relationship of man to
man, than the war of thctwo great classes of
capital and labour? I ask again, in the
name of our common Christianity, that alter-
nately weeps over, and emphatically condemns
this gigantic source of misery and evil, how
long is it to last? Can Christianity grow io
this moral waste? Nay, can it exist at all,
except in name. Impossible! As well might
wo e4peot figs to grow on thorns' or grapes on
thistles. Then let us pravail on those wlao are
anxious abvut the uwral and religious pro-

34

geikisi of hunianity, to thoroughly .retiltie-
vital importance of this suhject—the present
relation of capital and labour.
We have threaded the nation ardain with
neW and wonderful roads, bringing distaut
toivus and people into close proximity,' and
with the miraculous telegraph that traWries
both sea and hind, nation can speak with tiot
like neighbour with neighbour. We 'Make
communieation from sea to sea; that before
bad been separated by leagues of country, so
that our idhips might go direct from oecan to
ocean. We send our railways through arid
over the very mountains Of the earth. By
these, and a hundred °tar wondrous works,
we increase and extend world-wide thejfect-
procal communication of humanity, ,and:rmi-
mount the mighty physical obstacle i tse
brotherhood of man. i3ut other obstlieletl will

atop the way, and among the most formidable
is the present
.relation between capital and
labour.
We have invented mechanical and chemical
powers for the produotion of food, clothing,
and shelter, equal to the labour of hundreds
of millions of men, so that the tecessarieeand
amenities of life, under sensible aritingements,
could be made As plentiful as water. .
Thus we hae been wonderfully successful
in bur work upon physical nature; yet,
astounding to Say, we fail to place capital and .
labour, of -Which these wonders are the reaUlts,
in such relationship to each other, s, like the
parts of a well-constructed maohinc,, they
might work harmoniously together.; ot "like
kindred drOpsoningle into one."
There are two modes by which capita and
lab Our may he united and varied ecieordftig to .
circumstances; one is by eapifietlikiug
labour 'into partnership avith itizia -at 'Mr.
Bnfoas's co-operative collier?, neat Wakefield,
CROSSVEN:3B •Cnrpet Inft/infac dry, 'Halifax, an,d
Many others, giving labour a fixed Percentage
upon the profits it has assisted to create, and
which it. is as morally wrong to keep back
as to keep bank part of its wages,
The Other mode Is- for labaz&tii become its
own capitalist--,or, in other words, for liimur
to beConier capitedisttlatis making
titer interest eke; • Of course thig could not
be done by labour individually ; but in associa-
tion it is, perfectly practieable as tit the 'co-
operative farms comineneedpy , Mr. VAR..
DELEUR I
, 'County Clare, Ireland. The
co-operative farms of- Mr. GUERDON, which
have now been in the most successful operation
for more * than thirty, years at A:)sington,
Suffolk; the co-operative engine works, Ouse-
burn, Newcastle ; and Many ethers both
in .England, Scotland, on the Continent,
and in America. On this latter system
in which labour is its Qwn capitalist,
capital and labour will of course Ivor,: more
harmoniously then on the former sy4ein, in
which capital takes labour into palticrship.
There is more of the higher principle in it that
we call co-pperative ; it is a more perfect.
Machine, and, therefore, will there be. las
jarring ill its different parts. •
13oth these systems, however, of uniting
capital with labour will be attended with the
happiest results, if honestly and wisely carried.
out. Antagonisth or strikes, with all their.
train of moral and .physi:oal evils, would of
necessity cease.; there Would also ,be mero.
wealth produced, which has been incontestably
proved at Mr. BILIGGS'S eolliery,,and, therefore, .
there would be more to divide between capital;
and labour. „ .
. That labour can raise sufficient capital for
its own employment it is necessary to attempt
to prove. Millions of capital or its represen-
tatives pass through :the hands of: labour
weekly, and tho, smallest amount individually
reserved, and used co-operatively and wisely,
would attain the much- desired object. Labour
has raised millions to carry on.uunatural wars
with capital, though generally necessary under
the circumstances ; it has .millions iu the
saying's banks, Odd Fellows', Foresters', trade,
and other societies, which reflects great honour
on, the working classes; yet, in the face of
these facts, it is discreditably dependent , upon .
other men's capital for its employment. ,
What should we think of the carpenter hiring
his tools at an extortionate price from the
capitalist, when he could command the means
of purchasing them for himself?
Should we not think. him an improvident
simpleton? 'Yet we, too, the .great labour
' class ef: this ceuntry, pay the capitalist most
foolishly and extortionately. for giving .113.•
leave to toil with his capital. Have
we not produced all the geed clothing
and shelter in this immensely rich country ?
Yet in consequence of hiring our labour to the
capitalist, are we not the worst fed, the wont
clothed, and the worst sheltered, to such a
degree that the averageduration of our
is out short by ten years less than the average
duration of the lives °falter classes of !moiety ?
Nay, do net (and let, us. thoroughly realise the
fact), we, the groat labour class of,theliatjoa,
with our dear wives .and children, make, our-
selvea . dependant 'upon the , capitalia Laa4s
(whose interest is just. opposite to 'our own),
for our very bread,. aye,. for our very lives
And has nut this class, or rathar this system
(for. -we should do the same under the tialllEr
system), in innumerable instances, locked us
but from their capital, with the. elteruattve of
itarving in the streets, or working at stem a-

4

tion prices? Surely we do not at all realise
the great folly, the great wickedness of this
barbarous state of things, or we should put an
end to it at once and for ever.
We set about our daily work with laborious
toil and painstaking skill, we fashion and erect
the ponderous engine, make all its parts work
on the co-operative principle with and for each
other without a jar; and we have only to
apply the same painstaking and skill, and
persistent perseverance, to build up a higher
and more righteous relation between capital
and labour, that shall bless instead of curse
humanity, and practically supersede tins
senseless and immoral and fearfully unchris-
tian strife between capital and labour.
It is no use wasting our energies in con-
demning the capitalist, for, as I have intimated
before, if we changed places we should do the
same.
It is the system that is a great perversion of
wisdom and goodness; and, therefore, great
moral and physical miseries are of necessity its
results. Our business, then, is to change the
system from a scrambling intolerable anta-
gonism, that more befits the lower animals, to
one that is in accordance with tho advanced
and advancing state of man. Is it not dis-
creditable nay, is it not criminal? Ought we
not to despise ourselves for allowing this
state of things to go on year after year, when,
if we applied the will that we apply to our
everyday work, we could make it a thing of
the past.
To the glorious pioneer work, then, bro-
thers and sisters of this great march of labour
—of humanity, to a better, a higher state of
things! There are many difficulties in the
way; but we must be united, and of a noble,
self-saerifieing spirit, and we shall surmount
them all. We have the wisest and best of the
past and present in the ranks—aye, GOD him-
self for our co-worker, who will say, "Well
done, good and faithful servant," if we faint
not. We have only to will it, and this great
evil of antagonism between capital and labour
will disappear like the mist before the morning
sun.
There are many obstacles to be removed in
the path of human progress, but some of the
most
.pressing work before us at the present
tune is the unity of capital and labour.

Mr. H. Gover, who has been elected as in-
presentative for the Greenwich division, in the
place of the Rev. Canon Miller, D.D., resigned,
was introduced and took his seat. Mr.
M'Cireeror brought up a report from the In-
dustrial Schools Committee on the best means
of dealing with the ease of snob children of the
poorest or most improvident classes of London
as are deprived of education through the ex-
treme poverty or neglect. of their parents or
guardians, or who are unable to attend school
from lack of food. The report, after some
cutision, was rceeived.
In the course of the proceedings, the Rev.
°anon Cromwell moved, "That a return be
made of the various Committees and sub-
commit tees of the Board in existence on the
6th of May inst., with a description of their
respective duties, the names of the members
serving upon them, and the days on which
they meet."
Mr. Chatfeild Clarke, in seconding the
motion, suggested that the chief clerk should
put himself in communication with the
authorities of the Post-office and other large
establishments, in order to ascertain how
business was managed, with a view to the
reduction of labour. Mr. 'Freeman did not
see what wits to become Of the motion unless
the Board was prepared to abdicate its
functions. What lie thought was wanted was
a paid chairman, a thorough praetical or-
ganizer, who would give his whole time and
energies to the work of the Board. (Hear,
hear.) The actual Board basiness should be
carried out by members of the Board itself,
for that .was the object for which the rate-
payez a elected them; and he held it to be a
great delusion to suppose that they could in
any way imitate the Post-office. (Hear, hear.)
The Rev. Dr. Rigg said the pressure arising
from attendance on committees and sub.-com-
mittees was growing more onerous every day,
and he thought that in suggesting a paid
chairman Mr. Freeman had pointed out the
only remedy. It was impossible that they
could go on from month to month as they
were doing now.
Mr. Tabrum strongly objected to the ap-
pointment of a paid chairman, and hoped they
would adhere to the resolution adopted at the
first meeting of the Board, that the chairman
should be an honorary officer. The business
of the Board had been most admirably
managed by the chief clerk (Hr. Croad) and his
assistr uts.

A frer sorao further discussion the return Was
ordered.

Several managers and visitors for various
districts were appointed, aud the Board ad-
journed until Wednesday next.

LONDON.
THE SEAMEN'S AGITATION.

A numerously attended meeting of London sea-
men, including those in the service of the General
Steam Navigation Company, and convened by the
London Seamen's Mutual Protection Society, took
place on Friday night at the Horselydown Tavern,
Horselydown, "to take into consideration the
present rate of wages out of the port of London."
Mr. Lyons, the chairman, having explained the
objects of the society, and urged all who were not
members to enrol themselves,
Mr. Chipperton said the General Steam Naviga-
tion Company had offered them an additional 28, a
week, but even that would, no doubt, be taken off
again before twelve months passed over, unless
they held themselves together. The extra throe
hours they were engaged on loading nights, how-
ever, had not been taken off, and, were he to con-
sult his own individual interests, he would rather
sell the bed from under him than &wept that paltry
concession ; but they had to consider a numerous
body of married men who would nbt, perhaps,
take their stand with thern determinedly upon
their original demand, and therefore he thought it
would be better to accept the 258., and not turn
out.

Mr. Wynne then moved, " That this meeting is
of opinion that some action should be taken with a
view of bringing the shipowners ant the seamen
together for the purpose of having a fixed rate of
wages for all vessels sailing out of the port of Lon-
don, and therefore respectfully calls upon the ship-
owners to convene a meeting, at an early date,
and to receive a delegate: from the society as a
representative of the seamen."
Mr. Leman said that unless they were backed
by substantial power, their delegate would be
pooh-poohed. 137 moderation they could achieve
great things. Ho believed there was a general
feeling amongst shipowners that something must
be done, and if the seamen could elevate themselves
without any extraneous assistance so much the
better.
Mr. Dearing proposed the substitution of "a
deputation" in lieu of "a delegate," which was
seconded by Mr. Giles, and the resolution is
amended was than agreed to unanimously. After
some discussion it was further resolved, that in
the event of the shipowners acceding to the terms
of the previous resolution the deputation should he
invested with full powers to act on behalf of the

CARMEN AND THEIR WAGES.

On Sunday, at Winchester Ha.ll,•Pentonville, a
meeting, composed exclusively of railway carmen,
numbering little short of 600, was convened for the
purpose of taking into consideration the circum-
stance of the discharge of two of their number
from their employ, and of receiving the reports of
about 40 delegates who had waited, upon the rail-
way companies and firms, to request an advance of
2s. per week in the rate of wages, making the same
255., instead of 235., as at present. A number of
carmen addressed the meeting, and, as far as could
be gathered, it wonld appear that while Messrs.
Pickford and ;Co. and Messrs. Chaplin and Horne
have decided to.pay their men of the Ist class 2684,
2nd class 218., 3rd ;class 235, and so on, the
maximum rate being 2s more than the men have
been in the habit of receiving, the other firms and
the railway companies have neglected to return a
formal answer, or have absibitely objected to in-
troduce any change. The two men discharged are
said to have had the ignominy put upon them in
consequence of the part they .have taken in the
present agitation. One of the men named Mayhew
informed the meeting that the. entire body of their
fellow carmen in Messrs. Hawkins's employ were
prepared to "come out" if he and his mate. were
not permitted again to "ge in ; " but he put it to
those present whether that course were or wore not
preferrahle to the establishment of an organization
embracing the whole of the metropolitan carmen
for mutual support. It was ultimately, agreed at
once to form a society and establish a fund for the
support of the two men by a general levy of 2d..
per head. It was also agreed to hold a conference
on Sunday week, with the view of effecting the
object of the combination, viz., higher wages and
fewer hours.

WOOLWIMI.
THE NINE lIOURS MOVEMENT AT TUE ROYAL

ARSENAL.

A meeting of workmen belonging to the Royal
Arsenal at Woolwich, W as held on Plumstead-
common on Saturday afternoon, to -consider tho
propriety of memorialising the Government for
a reduction in the hours of labour. A division of
opiuiou bad grown up within the last few days

among the men themselves owing to a prevalent
report, apparently well authenticated, that the
Government were prepared at once to concede the
nine hours, but would at the same time abolish all
privileges—these privileges consisting of five
regular (and occasional extra) days' holiday in the
year, with pay, allowances of half-pay in sickness,
and full-pay if injured, the Saturday half-
holiday, &c. Nine-tenths of the workmen also
are employed on piece-work, and many dreaded
the decrease of pay which would follow if the hours
were reduced without the rate of payment being
augmented. .

Mr. Allen, an iron-moulder, took the chair,
and read the memorial which it was proposed to
present to the Controller-in-Chief, praying for a
reduction in the hours of labour from ten to nine
per day, and six on Saturdays, with an advance of
10 per cent. on piece-work where necessary.
IE% Lucas, an:engineer, moved the adoption of
the memorial; and said that previous to the intro-
duction of the nine hours system the arsenal men
worked 56 hours per week, which was supposed to
place them on a level with the men in private
yards, who, though they worked 58S hours, had
higher wages. The hours of labour had now been
generally reduced to 51 per week, being 41 loss
per week; and all they asked the Government for
was five hours, to place them on the same footing,
their wages and all other conditions remaining as
at present.

Mr. W. M'Cubry, a storoholder in the Control
Department, seconded the resolution, saying that
the natural division of the day was eight hours for
work, eight hours for recreation, and eight hours
for sleep.

Mr. -Lloyd Jones then addressed the meeting,
stating that the nine hours movement was a
necessary consequence of the increased demand for
labour, and that the workman was bound to sell it
on the best terms he could demand. He would act
consider the matter of wages at present; the
matter of time was of far more importance, for by
reducing the time they removed part of the com-
modity out of the market, and so increased its
value. If they lessened the hours, wages must rise.
Mr. Baxter Langley was the next speaker, and
road a letter from Professor Beesly, who sympa-
thised with the movement, and said that the State
workshops ought to be patterns for all the private
establishments to follow. Mr. Langley expressed
an opinion that the memorial would be granted,
and urged the workmen not to be afraid of asking
because Government might take away a holiday or
two and certain privileges which they could buy
cheaper of the Odd Fellows and Foresters.
Rev. G. Webb, of Plumstead Tabernacle, al so
addressed the meeting in support of the resolution,
which was then carried almost unanimously.
A vote of thanks to the speakers closed the pro-
ceedings.

TIIE UNITED. COOPERS' SOCIETY.

The following memorial has been sent to the
master coopers :

Stn,—We, the undersigned coopers at the
present time employed by you, do respectfully desire
to bring to your notice that on the 17th day of the
present month the coopers employed by the three
great cement manufacturers of Northfieet, did
receive an advance in the price of their work of
one halfpenny per cask made from new timber.
Therefore, Sir, we, your workmen, do respect-
fully solicit a like boon—viz., one halfpenny per
cask made from new timber.
We make the solicitation:for three reasons—
First-13ccause a reduction of one penny per
cask was made by cement merchants and master
coopers four years ago.

• Second—Because we desire if possible to reduce
the hours of our laborious toil in order that
we may have some healthful recreation • for the
body, and more time for the improvement of the
mind. .

Third—Because every article of production is
augmenting in price, a fact which we fear will
hinder us from becoming much -better off even
with the original prices we received four years
ago.
Trusting that this request will meet with a
favourable 'reception by you, Sir, we, the uuder-
signed shop's company, hereby give you a fair
week's notice that we 'shall expect an answer either
written or verbal by Friday, the 31et day of the
present month. Further, we beg to state our
request and your answer shall be duly published
in the BEE-11ms newspaper for the information of
the employers of coopers and others.
Signed by the whole of the men.

DERBY.

VIZ STRIKE OP OPEL'ATIVE SPINNEII3.

At the time I write, the strike of operative
spinners has not, yet come to a satisfactory ter-
mination. The public papers here contain a short

MAY 31, 1872.

pivagraph, stating that "the strike of operative
spinners is virtually at an end, females being now
employed in place of the men." This statement
is calculated to mislead many, people, allowing
them to infer that the females can do the same
quantity of work as the men. Now I utterly
deny females being capable of doing any of the walk
as well as the men cat; and moreover three of
them can do nothing like the quantity that ono
man was previously doing.

That the masters should employ females "°
place of the men is no surprise to anybody, for
they appear capable of the very meanest action for
even two farthings an hour; but that they should
find females willing to be their dupes and serve
their purposes is to be wondered at, and I ara
sorry that females are to be found mean enough to
do such a disgraceful and contemptible action
amongst my own townspeople, though there is
some satisfaction in knowing they are of the
lowest grade. I still maintain that the success of
the men is certain, providing they will be as firm
as they appear at the present time, and it would
be well for them to teach these " nobsticks
they are dubbed—a short and sharp lesson by re"
fusing to go to work until they are dismissed.
And for the benefit of their" gleam of the future,'
I might venture to say there is some probabilitY
of them being fixed in this uncomfortable and
vexatious dilemma, besides being shunned and
held up to derision and contempt by every respect-
able and honest person.

At a meeting last Saturday the mon unani-
mously resolved to adhere to tho original demand,
and accept nothing less, viz., two shillings per week,
with time and quarter time for all overtime. Re-
marking that the mutual concession named in the
BEE-HIVE might have been acceptable at the first
onset, the above-mentioned paper came in for a
good share of praise from all parties for the
justice that has been allowed them in its columns
front the commencement of the strike.

It appears that the employers have been bound
over to forfeit a large sum of money if any of them
should succumb to the demands of the men before
a stipulated time, and I am informed thet the term
of the bond expired on Wednesday last, the 29th
ult., therefore it is almost probable some definite
understanding will be come to before long.
The finances of the Silk Throwers' Union are very
promising, and still rapidly on the increase; in-
deed it is rumoured they intend raising the pay-
ment of the men. which will, at least, have two
very good effects.
The Town Council have proposed that arrange-
ments shall be made at the union for some of the
men, women, and children on strike and out of
employment. It is an excellent idea, and worthy
of consideration; it would serve so well for the
poor female aspiring spinners that will be so
mercilessly thrown out of work. If either the
men, women, or children had been left to the
tender mercies of their class, they might have
sought relief in the place that they, as well as
Town Councillors or Derby employers, help to
maintain for the good of all that are "hungry and

require rest."
On Saturday, upwards of 700 of the hands in
the rotary branch of the hosiery trade now .ori
strike at Nottingham met to hear the reply of Mr.
S. Morley, M.P., to the deputation which was
appointed to wait upon him in order to arrive, if
possible, at a settlement of their dispute. The
interview was reported to have been of an amicable
nature, and Mr. Morley promised to endeavour to
procure the formation of a board amongst the
masters for the settlement of the present dispute,
and he expressed his deep regret that such a
rupturo should have ever occurred. Ultimately
it was agreed by the workmen to form a council
to meet the masters, the deputation to be chosen
out of twenty men selected from each of the dif-
ferent factories.

TIER SILK THROWERS' STRIKE.

To the Editor of the Bas-Itive.

Sin,—The Derby papers are informing the
public that the strike is virtually at an end, as
women are doing the men's work. I will give you
the facts. In the first place, the employers are
paying twelve to fourteen shillings per week to
women, and it takes front two to three women to
do one man's work, and the quantity is far inferior
to that of the men, and this they do with tb°
avowed purpose of crushing our union. They have
also scoured the country round for men to Mice our
places, but they have only succeeded in obtaining
five men, and they left the town as soon as they
found out the true state of affairs in Derby. Now,
if women could do our work in 0. manner that
would pay, it is plain they would not exert themselvea so much to obtain men; besides, they are
inviting men to work that they would not eraploY
upon any consideration but for the present diffi-
culty, and, us a last resort, they have disoh?rgad
the men's wiyes, children, and other relatives

because the men would not return to work at the
old price, thus showing the baseness of the asser-
tion that women can do our work in anyway satis-
factory. Sir, lam happy to inform you that the
men are firm, in spite of the intimidation the
employers have used, and determined to stand out
until their just rights are conceded. Hoping
these few facts will enlighten the public as to
the true state of affairs in Derby, I remain, yours
respectfully, A SPINNER.
Derby, May 27th.

CAMBRIDGE.
)-WILDING OPERATIVES' STRIKE.

The carpenters, bricklayers, and labourers are
still on strike, this making the fifth week. Not
any offer whatever has been made by the employers
since the strike commenced. A meeting of the
men was held last Wednesday, when it was
unanimously resolved to stand out until our reason-
able demands are conceded. We regret to say we
have not received oven a little support from our
fellow workman of other towns.—Yours respect-
fully,

J. IL Coma, Chairman.
Black Swan, Guildhall-street.

LEICESTER.
TICE TRUCE ACT.

• A meeting of working men was held in
the Temperance Hall, Leicester, on Monde y
evening last, to take into consideration the
Master and Servants' Wages Bill, as amended in
Select Committee. The chair was occupied by
Mr. T. P. Bailey, a framework knitter. There
was a fair attendance. The chairman having
opened the meeting at great length, in which lie
expressed his approval of the Act, called upon
Mr. Daniel Merrick, also a framework knitter, to
move the first resolution, which he did as follows:
—"That, in the opinion of this meeting, the
Master and Servants' Wages Bill, as amended in
Select Committee, is deserving the support of the.
working classes generally, as it fully secures the
abolition of frame rents and charges, and renders
illegal all stoppages from the wages of working
men, except in such cases as are specified in
clause 8, and even these do not appear inconsistent
with the principles of the Bill." In speaking on
this motion, he referred to the Bills introduced last
session by Mr. A. Pell and Mr. Mundella, road
over clause 8, and expressed his concurrence with
it, and the Bill generally, except the portion of
clause 8 which referred to the fines. That he
termed the weakest part of the Bill, as he did not
like stoppages for not keeping time from men who
"have what they earned." Men receiving so
much per day he thought ought to be fined for
not keeping to their time. This motion was
seconded by Mr. Robert Brindley, supported by
Mr. Pegg, and carried unanimously.
Mr. Flude then proposed, "That this mooting
desires to express its thanks to her Majesty's
Government for bringing in the present Bill, and
also to the Select Committee for their amendments
made therein, and respectfully urges them not to
relax their efforts until the same Bill is passed into
law." 1.4, Howard seconded this motion, and Mr.
Hartshorn, of Thurraaston, supported it, and it
was unanimously carried.
The next resolution was moved by Mr. James
Merrick, and was as follows :—" That the fore-
going resolutions be signed by the chairman on
behalf of this meeting, and that copies of it be
forwarded to the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone
and Mr. Bruce, the Home Secretary. Also to the
Borough and County Members, and Messrs. Mor-
ley and Mundella, with an earnest desire that they
will support the same." This motion was seconded
by Mr. Sharp, supported by Mr. Henson, and also
unanimously carried,
A question from the body of the hall was asked
as to whether it would touch the rivetters. Tho
chairman could not say, but believed it provided a
remedy for all the evils in the existing trades. H
it did not do justice to any trade it was the duty of
the trade to urge upon the Government or the
Select Committee to provide some remedy for
them.

Tho meeting closed with a. vote of thanks to the
Chairman.

NORTHAMPTON.
TIIE CARPENTERS AND PAINTERS.

The following code of working rules have been
adopted by the employers and employed in the
carpentering and painting trades of Northampton,
to come in operation on the Ibt of Tune, 1872.
That the employers agree to reduce the hours of
lobour to 54 per week, and to pay to the workmen
the same amount of wages for the 54 hours as they
pay for the present working week ; and that 3UCh
wages shall in future be paid by the hour.
That 91 hours be considered a day's work ;
commencing each day at G a.m., and to cease at
6 p.m., except on Saturday, when work shall
ceaso at 1; making a total of 64 hours per week.

That overtime to the extent of two hours be
worked, if necessary, after the 91 hours the first
five days, and two hours after the 61 on Saturday;
and that the rate of wages for such overtime be at
the ordinary rate. If necessary to work beyond
that time, the employers to pay at the rate of
time-and-half.

That when the job does not exceed one mile
from the shop, the men shall walk in their own
time; but if it exceed one mile, walking time to
and fro at the rate of three miles per hour beyond
tha

I distance up to three miles; from three to
twelve miles, railway faro or other conveyance,
lodgings to be allowed and time to return once a
week; and from twelve to twenty miles, once a
fortnight. Over that distance, arrangements must
be made between employers and employed.
-That payment of wages commence at one
o'clock on Saturday and be completed at two
o'clock; and if not completed by that time, the
men may charge the time over as if at work.
That 4.L- hours' notice shall be given by the em-
ployer or the workman of any intention to
put an end to their services ; and that such notice
shall expire at the end of such working day. In
default thereof either party shall forfeit 41. hours'
pay; but if any infringement of these rules be
attempted, no notice shall be required. This rule
does not apply to any but those who have worked
six days for employer.
That three months' notice be given by either
party concerned if any alteration ta the above
rules is required.
That the alterations proposed come into opera-
tion the Ist day of June, 1872.

SOUTH STAFFORDSHIRE.

TILE PROPOSED GREAT UNION OF IRONWORICERS.

On Monday a large meeting of ironworks opera-
tives was held at Bilston, South Staffordshire, in
promotion of the union which is proposed to em-
brace all operatives engaged in ironworks
throughout the kingdom. Mr. A. Walker, the
chairman of the operatives' delegates, who form
half the Conciliation Board in the iron industry of
South Staffordshire, presided. He said that the
Sheffield Conference had been convened by the
Staffordshire men because they had received com-
munications from South Wales, and other distant
parts of the kingdom, urging them to be very eare-
ful as to what they did, because what was done in ,
Staffordshire influenced every other iron-making
industry. Now that the views of the other districts
had been obtained through the Sheffield Confe-
rence, they know how to proceed when, a few days
hence, they would again have •to meet their
masters, and to agree upon the wages to be paid
in the ensuing six months. But in order to their
success at the forthcoming meeting, all the opera-
tives must show that they were determined to have
what they believed was justice. Hence it became
impoitant that branches of the National Amalga-
mated Ironworkers' Association should be estab-
lished at every works in the kingdom. The
meeting adopted a resolution to establish branches
in that district.

BELFAST.
TUB STRIKE IN TILE I,LAIi. TRADES.

There is a Horious danger of a great strike in the
flax trials at Belfast. It is stated that, "in less
than a fortnight, according to all present appear-
ances, between 30,000 and 35,000 people will be
idle in Belfast." A btriko or lock-out of such
gigantic proportions has never hitherto been
known in Ireland.

LEEDS.
THE CIUMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT.

On Saturday a numerously-attended meeting of
delegates from the various trades of Leeds and
district, was hold at Parker's Temperance Hotel,
Briggate, Leeds, to consider the propriety of hold-
ing a demonstration in favour of the repeal of the
Criminal Law Amendment Act.
The following trades were represented .at the
meeting !...--Arnalganutted engineers (two branches),
carpenters and joiners, bakers, ironfounders (two
branches), plasterers, locomotive engineers, brush.
makers, woollen spinners, steam-engine makers,
smiths, masons, bookbinders, cloth prossers, tailors,
hammermen, bricklayers, cloth dressers, coach-
makers, tin-plate workers, wheelwrights, stone-
masons, millers, willeyers and fAtlers, paper
stainers, papers makers,cabinet makers, bricklayers'
labourers, glass bottle makers, and representatives
of the -felt trade.

Mr. E. C. Denton, joiner, president of the
Council, occupied the chair.
- The Chairman said that the meeting was called
for the purpose of ascertaining from the members
of the - different trades societies in the district
whether or not it was desirable to do something
more than had been hitherto accomplished in the
direction of procuring a repeal, or at least an
alteration, of the obnoxious clauses of the Criminal
I,IIW Amendment Act.

The Secretary of the Council (Kr. Thomas
Placket, coaehmaker) read a digest and report of
the Trades Union Acts and the Amendment Act,
and stated that 32 prosecutions had been tried
under these provisions.
Mr. George Panther, brushmaker, proposed that
a demonstration should be held in Leeds; two
meetings in towns like Leeds and Bradford must
have considerable weight with those who would
be engaged in the alteration of the law. Mr.
Bannister, willeyer and fettler, seconded the pro-

position.

A. delegate asked if it was not possible to unite
with Bradford in holding a joint West Biding de-
monstration? (Hear, hear.)
The Chairman replied that the Council had
every reason to believe that the Bradford com-
mittee had completed their arrangementl4. Their
list of speakers seemed to have been filled up, as it
was stated that Mr. George Potter and Mr.
Howell were going to attend as a deputation from
London.

Mr. Lishman, after some further discussion, in
which the relative merits of a public meeting or a
demonstration were debated, proposed an amend-
ment to the effect that, instead of holding a de-
monstration, a mass meeting should be held. Mr.
Roach, bricklayer's labourer, seconded the amend-
ment. The amendment and resolution were then
submitted to the meeting, when there was a
majority of six or seven in favour of holding an
outdoor demonstration,

Mr. D. Sheard, willeyer and fettler, proposed
that the demonstration should consist of a proces-
sion to Woodhouse Moor and a public meeting.
Mr. Panther seconded the resolution, which was
carried.

It was determined to hold the demonstration on
Saturday, the 22nd of Juno; and a committee of
management having been appointpd, the con-
ference adjourned until June 15th.

THE MINERS.

MtETING OF MINERS, LARK HALL, SCOTLAND.

On Thursday, the 23rd inst., a mass meeting of
the miners of Lark Hall, was held neer the town.
The object of the mooting was to take into con-
sideration the amended payment of wages. One
of the workmen presided. Mr. McDonald
addressed the meeting at considerable length on
the new form of the Payment of Wages Bill. He
condemned all the changes nearly in the procedure
of the committee. It was agreed to send a
memorial to the Home Secretary, the Right
Honourable Henry A. Bruce, asking him, if
possible, to make the payment of wages weekly,
and that without any deduction. It was also
agreed to ask Major Hamilton, M.P., to support
the views of the meeting.

MEETING IN THE COUNTY OP STERLING, N.B.

On Monday, the 27th inst., a great meeting of
the miners of the above-named county was held
in Baulkine's Hall, Falkirk. There were re-
presentatives present from all the organized
districts in Scotland. Mr. Webster, presided.
The meeting was addressed on the benefits of
union by Messrs. Penman, Hughes, Stopple, and
others. Mr. McDonald called the attention of
the meeting to the mutilated Payment of Wages
Bill. He personally considerred it an insult on
the common sense of the nation. It was unani-
mously agreed to send a remonstrance to the
Home Secretary, Mr. Bruce, on the subject, calling
upon hini to press that all wages be paid weekly
without any deduction therefrom. It was agreed
to unite the various sections of the county into one
general board.

FRIDAY, MAY 31, 1872.

SIDNEY SMITH AND THE IRON

TRADES.

IT will be seen from a circular published in
another column, that SIDNEY SIIITII,, who, at
the head. of the ironmasters some twenty years
ago, destroyed—as it was said—the Amalga-
mated. Engineers' Union, is in the field again.
The men whom ho met in battle in 1851 have
been in the field ever since ; they were then
10,000 members, with a fund amounting to
£2,000. They are now 39,000, with a reserve
fund of £138,000. They were at that time defec-
tive in organization and mutual reliance. They
are now not only overwhelmingly numerous, but
dangerous to the last degree by their higher
knowledge, more thorough discipline, and more
abundant resources. Besides, they have just
come out of their short-time fight victorious,
and will at any moment, should they deem it
necessary, be able to face the employers even
with this doughty gentleman at their head.
Nobody can blame the employers in any
branch of industry for going into union, and
few working men will care much whether
SIDNEY SMITH should be appointed to lead
them or not. If they carry into their union a
like desire to that of the men, for a quiet and
reasonable settlement of such differences as
may arise, they will find it much easier to
settle these by a general consideration and
decision than by that desultory individual
method which at present prevails amongst
them. A properly organized union amongst
the employers would be better for the men as
well as for themselves; that is, provided
always, that their dominant desire is for peace,
not for war—that their aim is to settle not to
disturb.

It must be confessed, however, that the
circular of SIDNEY SMITR is suspiciously
belligerent in its tone. The mouldy moth-
eaten nonsense about supply and de-
mand may be passed, over. In, a souse

MAY 31, 1872.

in which it is not understood by &MIT
SMITH, it is perfectly true. Hence the .
working men's unions, above all things,
aim at regulating demand and supply; and
it is clear that the proposed union of employers
means the same thing, though Mr. SMITH,
blinded by old formulas, don't see this. The
men, by their combinations, fight their em-
ployers by withholding the supply from the
labour market at a critical moment;
the masters, by this oracular mouth-piece of
theirs, talk of closing the labour market
against men on strike, both resorting to
analagous measures for a like end from their
opposing positions as sellers and buyers of
labour.

But we shall not attempt to mystify Mr.
SMITH on the question of demand and supplY•
It will be better and more humane to console
him on that of short hours. In glancitg at
this he almost groans in agony of spirit.
"Encroachments," he says, "have been
gradually made on the stated weekly hours of
work, until, from 60, they have been reduced
to 59, then to 54, now in extensive districts to
51, while it is openly avowed that the latter
limit is only a stage to a temporary terminus
of 48, with an absolute rise in the -rate of
wages."

This, surely, must foretoken the end of the
world; or, what would be worse, a Millennium
into which working men only were privileged
to enter. Shorter hours of work and more
pay must surely have something in it calcu-
lated to shock all " well-regulated minds ;'' and
possibly so monstrous a wickedness might be
turned from with horror by the men, if SIDNET
SMITH would benevolently undertake to point
out to them the wickedness of their ways.

Sixty hours a week is ten hours a day,
Saturday included. Is that the only orthodox
time? Why ten rather than nine? Why nine
rather than eight? Why eight in preference to
seven? Masters, we are told by Mr, Small, have
to meet "foreign competitors whose working
hours range from 60 to 72." Be it so; but, at
any rate, it is undeniable that so far they have
thoroughly beaten these competitors. Sup-
pose, however, that the British workman,
instead of running down to what Mr. SMITE
calls the "temporary terminus of 48 hours,'
should run back to the Continental terminus
of 72, will the employers' secretary give a
guarantee that the Continental people will not
go to 75 or 80, and thus render the foreign
competition relatively what it is at present ?
Let Mr. SMITE, however, look at this other
alternative, and take comfort from it. This
, is mentioned because the attempt is actually
on foot at the present time amongst Conti-
neutal work-people, namely, to reduce the
hours abroad, so as to bring them as near as
possible to the English level. With the
power of producing too much everywhere,
surely this is a better rivalry, commercially
as well as humanely, than that proposed
by the masters' secretary; at any rate, it is
that into which the working men are most ,
likely to enter on. It may not be quite respect-
ful, but it is much more likely that the work-
ing men will take the advice of their own
leaders in preference to that of Swim SAIITII,
who speaks for employers, and even at the
risk of being charged with opposing them-
selves as a class against their employers, they
will persist, we believe, in helping each other.
The compositors contributing to the masons'
and carpenters' strike, shocks Mr. SUM/. The
levy of .000 made by the Amalgamated
Engineers for the Warwickshire agricultural
labourers confounds his "five wits." But
will Mr. SMITE say whether printers and
publishers, builders and contractors, farmers
or landlords, are worse off for this? As an
employing class, have they been injured? and if
not, why cry out in alarm on their
behalf ? Under such circumstances Mr. Shorn
will no doubt succeed in making the employers
thoroughly dissatisfied with their position.
Possibly a number of them may give up
mastership, and enter the workshops as arti-
zans that they may enjoy the privilege of short
hours and high wages. At least it is to be '
pected—unless SIDNEY Sum" can, by Owl
new organization, put an effectual cheek oil the
unions—a large number will take their Calgtal
to foreign countries that they may revel in the
profit flowing in from the labour of a bappb

industrious people, who:whistle and sing over
their work from 60 to 72 hours every week.

Suppose we put a case in point,—that the
provocation of the employer to run away with
his money from England may be understood.
Mr. %Hilt, in this oiroular of his, professes to
not for the "Iron Trades Employers' Associa-
tion," and will therefore understand the cal-
culation we make here. Looking at the price
of bar iron in the English market for the last
thirty years, it will be found that its lowest
price was in 1851, when it sold at an
average over the whole year of £5 lie. 6d.
per ton. The prioe of the same article at
this moment is from £lO 103. to .ell 55., ac-
cording to quality. If we take the lowest
price in 1851 as cost of production, and it was
certainly not more than that, and add now 10
per cent. as an advance on wages, which will
make the cost of production slightly higher,
what, we ask, becomes of the difference of, say,
£5 per ton as enhanced price? If it does not
go into the manufacturer's pocket, where does
it go? Mr. SUITIE is clever at calculation,
and ought to be able to tell—will he do so?
Or perhaps he will inform us in what foreign
country an ironmaster can get more profit on
his money.
No, no, the ironmaster will not take his
capital out of the country with the view of
getting more profit. If so, he is very likely
to" go out for wool and come home shorn.'
The ironmasters of England will never
permanently leave this country to go any-
where but to heaven, and when they must
leave us finally they have our warmest wishes
for their moan in finding the home they
desire. If they miss their way and get on
the path that slopes downwards, it is not at all
unlikely that their unpleasant journey and its
"terminus," which will not be "temporary,"
may be duo to doctrines and practices in rela-
tion to their workers which put the true human
duties of justice and kindliness below those
false ones of mastership and greed, and which
helped them to pile up wealth without duly
considering the welfare of those by whose
labour it was put into their coffers.
We would recommend to SIDNEY SMITH,
however,—should he not find profitable em-
ployment for his energies in connection with
the ironmasters,—that he should see what he
can do for the " misuses " in helping to
suppress the demands for more wages and
shorter time amongst the "servant gals."

THE LONDON BUILDING TRADES AND
THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.

Tun London Building Trades are once more
In a critical condition. This day has been
anxiously looked for all the week. The
crowded and strengthened attendance at the
adjourned meeting last Saturday was pre-
monitory to the masters, who were so far
affected by the firm attitude of the men as to
reicind their resolution against receiving de-
putations. One of the masters principally
concerned thinks 'the demands of the men
unconscionable," but they cannot be dia.
posed of by strong epithets. The attitude of
the men was sufficiently shown when, instead
of contenting themselves with instructing the
deputation of seven to stick to the fifty-one
hours at ninopence an hour, they carried, by
a large majority, a prudential resolution re-
stricting the power of the deputation to
simply hearing and reporting to a future
meeting any proposal made by the Masters'
Committee.

In the agricultural distriets the first attempt
at an understanding between masters and
men has come to nothing. Aftier three hours
spent in conference, the Warwiekshire
Chamber of Agriculture and the Labourers'
Union could not agree in any resolution. The
latter adhered to their requirements ; but.the
former, while admitting the right of the men
to unite, demurred to their proposals. The
Nottinghamshire Chamber of Agriculture
have made a formal deliverance on the whole
subject of disagreement. They have no object-
ten to matters being settled between masters
and men; but no third parties, especially
"paid agitators," must interfere; and, in
fact, the whole business must be "left to
Initiate itself by the law of supply and
demand." Translated into plain English,
this mane that "the weakest shall go to the

wall." On this occasion, there was a Duke in
the chair. His speech was as plausible as could
have been expected, and his conclusion such as
might have been predicted from the lips of a
landowner of the first rank. His Grace of St.
ALBANS deprecated tyranny and "stamping
out." Tr, indeed, the labourers met at beer-
shops, the result would be something awful ;
but, if they simply showed " a sense of greater
responsibility," the ease would be different.
At all events, landlords and occupiers must
not wince. The condition of their labourers
I would have to be looked into. One thing was
certain—Whatever wages they had, must be
paid in money. If they got an increase,
though, whence was it to come? Out of rents?
That would deprecate landed property. The
real question was, whether the loss would fall
upon producer or consumer. In his opinion,
the consumer would have to bear it. Now, it
is easy for a Duke to speak of wages fairly
earned as "loss" to the payers, and to put
that loss upon the consumer, which means a
higher price of meat and bread, as if they are
not dear enough already; but we take the
liberty of saying in return, that the labourer
is worthy of his hire; while DIVES, who wears
purple and fine linen and faros sumptuously
every day, must either learn to number it as
among the highest of his luxuries to see the
land maintaining in decent sufficiency and
comfort those who till it, or prepare for a
vigorous revision of the conditions on which
he holds his estates.

articles.title: VALUE OF A HAT.
articles.text:
THE VALUE OF A HAT.

TUE Cologne Gazette announces the death
at Colmar of a millionaire, who owed his wealth
to his hat. His story was as follows :—About
the year 1825, a poor turner, of the name of
MABEE, came barefoot, and carrying his knap-
sack, into the village wherein stood the
factory of Messrs. WEIL and BountoN,
machinists. On asking for employment, Herr
WEIL, who was not favourably impressed by
his ragged exterior, sent him about his busi-
ness. The workman bowed to adverse fate,
and went on his way sorrowfully. Suddenly
the machinist called him back. "Stop," said
he, "what sort of a hat is that you have on ? "
"It is a wooden hat, air." "A. wooden hat?
Let me see it better. Where did you buy
it ? " "I made it myself, sir." "And how
did you make it ? " "On the lathe, sir."
"On the lathe? But your hat is oval, and
everything turned is round ?" "That is
true," replied the workman, "but I have
made the hat by that means nevertheless; I
feigned the centre, and then turned as it
occurred to me; I have to walk far, and re-
quire a hat which shall serve me as an um-
brella, and as I have no money to buy one, I
had to make it." The poor workman, MABLE,
had instinctively discovered the eccentric
mode of turning, which was to be of such ex.
traerdinary importance in modern mechanics.
Herr WEn saw the enormous value
of the discovery with the quick per-
ception of an experienced manufacturer.
Ho kept the man with the wooden hat
by him, and found him not only a skilled
workman, but a genius to whose development
only opportunity and a very little cultivation
were required. The workman, MABLE, soon
took part in the profits of the business; he
lately became its proprietor under the name
of MouuN, and thus acquired the great
wealth he left behind him at his death.

articles.title: SUPPLEMENTARY ARTICLE.
articles.text:
THE SUPPLEMENTARY ARTICLE.

THE Senate of the United States has justi-
fied our forecast of the event. Not that we
pretend to the credit of prophecy, but that
we had faith in the ultimate triumph of sense
over—well, bunkum. The adoption of the
Supplementary Article in addition to the,Treaty
of Washington depended, by the American
Constitution, upon its having the support of
two-thirds of the Senators. Twenty-one were
either absent or abstained from voting and,
of the rest, forty-two voted yes, and nine only
no. Though the division was decisive, the
debate was long, occupying eight hours. The
speeches were animated; and the minority
full of chagrin. No matter: the result goes
to show that good feeling towards England
and the world which, notwithstanding all
occasional appearances to the contrary/ is, we

entirely believe, the sentiment of intelligent
and right-hearted America.
Before, however, we join in jubilee, let us
see the Article in the shape which it assumed
under the executive hands of the Senate.
Alterations were made; but, as we are as-
sured, these modify the phraseology of the
draft without affecting its substance and
meaning. Should comparison show this
assurance to be true, all nations having a
real desire to live at peace may join in general
congratulation. If, indeed, the changed
wording introduced has put the abandonment
of the Indirect Claims set forth in the American
Case in times of greater precision, and if, at
the same time, a wider scope has been given
to the provision by which, for the future,
neither America or England shall be liable, in
their relations with each other, to demands
for consequential damages arising out of
breaches of neutrality in time of war—in such
ease the Senate of the United States will have
acequired new titles to gratitude and respect.
We are now (Tuesday) hoping to be assured
by Earl GRANVILLE that the ratifications
have been exchanged, and the Supplementary
Article is become of binding force between us.
In the meantime, Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to
Mr. DISRAELI, has given some information.
On Monday, the Cabinet had the Article in the
amended form, approved by the American
Senate, for the first time before them. The
law-officers of the Crown had to be consulted
before the Government could have sent their
final agreement to the American Minister.
The modifications are as yet strictly confi-
dential, and under discussion; and, before
ratification, the conclusive arrangement must
pass both ways over the Atlantic. "I may
say," observed the PREMIER, "that not one
moment shall be lost in returning our reply to
the last proposal of the American Government,
so as to make our contribution towards pro.
duoing the consummation which both nations
so ardently desire."
To Mr. DISRAELI'S question, whether, be-

fore ratification, Ministers would submit the
Supplimentary Article to Parliament, Mr.
GLADSTONE answered, Yes, without ,hesitation
in circumlocution. Indeed, that answer was
so certainly foreseen, that the questioner was
fain to seek a reason for his inquiry in the n ow
mode of " negooiation by understanding,"
which, as he affected to think, the Government
had introduced. The PREMIER, however,
easily turned the soft point of this mild
sarcasm, the House endorsing his answer when
he said that he had not been accustomed to
defend the Treaty under consideration on the
ground of "understanding," but had, on the
contrary, been much blamed for declining to

do so. The moment, at any rate, the Treaty
is oonoluded, Parliament will be made ac-
quainted with its precise terms. At present
all the efforts of Government are directed
towards avoiding any contention by express
arrangement.
The stand made by the GLADSTONE Cabinet,
upheld by the hands of all parties in Parlia-
ment, has afforded an example to the who le
world of which Englishmen can feel honestly
proud. By firmness and moderation, by a
calm and dignified persistency, we have
carried a point in which, though British
policy required it at our hands, this country
has a greater interest than have the "United
States, nor either of those Powers than have
all the established Governments of the world.
In fact, the benefit will be universal; for
whatever tends to peace, tends to the chocking
of wrongful uses of foroe, not only between
nations called civilised, but also in all dealings
and intercourse between men and men even in
the wildest countries and among the most
primitive tribes.

It was as important that Canada should be
satisfied as that England should be guaranteed.
The Parliament of the Dominion has aeoepted
the Treaty by a majority tantamount to popular
approval. Those Amerioan claims which
affected the Canadians were referred for deci-
sion to the Colonial Legislature. The first
feeling was certainly not favourable. The
revival of the Reciprocity Treaty was rather
loudly called for; and then, there were the
Fishery question and the Fenian raids. If
for the deeds of steamers leaving English ports
*armed England was to bet held responsible,

how much more were the United States re-
sponsible for the outrages of men collected,
organized, and armed on American soil, and
led against the unoffending Canadians Yet,

the only use made of these facts was, to
strengthen our general ease against,the Indirect
Claims. " Her MAJESTY'S Government,"
wrote Earl GRAN VILLE to the American Ambas-
sador, "acquiesced in the proposal to exclude
from the negotiations their claims on behalf of
Canada against the United States for injuries
suffered from Fenian raids, partly from a desire
on their part to act in a spirit of conciliation,
and partly because a portion of these claims
was of a constructive and inferential
character."

This was so manifestly a concession that
nobody could be surprised if many of the
Canadians were unable to perceive any just
cause for making it. Nevertheless, when the
situation of the Dominion is considered, reason
will be found for applauding the polioy of its
Prime Minister in accepting the proposed
arrangement. England made sacrifices for
Canada, but Canada makes some for England;
and both, in doing justice to themselves,
confer benefits upon the entire world. The
guarantee of the Pacific) Railway was more
than any mere compensation in money; and
Parliament will freely consent to the loan of
two millions and a-half for its construction.

MORE BLOODSHED UNDER TRIERS.
Tuv. anniversary of the Defeat of the Com-
mune of Pelvis has been carefully marked with
blood. If M. Tunas was a consenting pal ty
to the shooting of three convicted Communists
on that anniversary (and it is not possible to
conceive of its taking place without his direct
privity), he has committed one of those
blunders which Prince TALLEYRAND branded
as worse than crimes. True, the three men
bad been found guilty of the murder of
several priests. But in what court and on
what evidence? Had the Party of Order
been sparing of blood, they might have been
severely just in dealing with adversaries
stained with blood. But we know too well
that their triumph was disgraced with
butcherly slaughter. From the wretched
exiles we know that oven their tender mercies
are cruel; and cannot, therefore, pretend sure

Will no Member of Parliament take up this

exposed with just indignation the Neapolitain

the first year of M. Timms' administration

three executed men were supposed to have

SIMMER and Boirr, were shot by files of
soldiery at Satory. A whole year of peace
intervenes, yet the THIERS Government must

righteously condemned, and worthily
