POLITICAL MEANS TO SOCIAL ENDS.
[Costatusucarms.]
THE friends of the working man are not
always agreed on the advice they shall 'give
him With a 'view to the improvement of his
social position, and it is curious to see how
many of them have, of late, hit upon the idea
of dissuading him from the pursuit of political
power as a means of securing social reforms;
This tendency is noticeable, not in England
only, but in France, Germany, and Italy. The
writer of these remarks, being one of those who
believes this new policy to be simply
suicidal, wishes to draw attention to the follow-
ing sentiments expressed by the E mane ipazione,
the organ of the Italian working men, with
regard to this question :—The first step towards
the emancipation of, the workman (says this
journal) Twist be the acquisition of universal
suffrage; the second, that of depriving ,tlie
executive power of the right of making peace Or
war ; restoring it to the people—the sole judge
and ruler of itself and its own interests. With
the, free exercise of that right, permanent
armaments, the instruments of tyranny and
arbitrary power, will be suppressed, and the
Only obstacle removed to the settlement of all
the political and economical questions which
agitate the Continental States. With the
abolition of standieg armies, and with universal
suffrage, the working-class will, like the middle
class, acquire liberty of association, of thought,
of expression, of coalition—the only practical
method by which salaried workmen can deal
with the proprietors of. capital and land.
Finally, the Ei§vereignty roast reside in all the
-
members of a nation, not in.a few privileged
mortals.. . . . Here is the knot of
the social question, which it is vain to
attempt aolving by eMpirical remedies.
We consider those who deny the existence of a
social question, and those who would, postpone
every other principle to the material 'well-
being, and economioal amelioration of the
operative caste as equally illogical, for they
move in a vicious circle. It is evident that
the first of these classes are- satisfied with
the present distribtition of fortune, because
they know not how much sweat, and how
many tears the scanty bread has cost with
which the workmen in factory or field is sup-
ported, or because they enjoy comforts easily
acquired and only accessible to a privileged
minority; hence they do not, or they will not,
see , that serious wrongs have to be redressed,
and that Much justice remains to he done to
the 'numerous filthily of producers As lo4g
as there is in Europe a political question--.and
this will exist as long as the present state of
things continues—there will, in like manner,
be a social queStien. Attempts are in vain
made to give society: a secure foundation; it
will not find peace, security, and order, if it
does not first give satisfaction to the moral
and material needs of the *orkmen. It, is a
question atone° of opportunity and of morality.
But it is impossible to introduce equal rela-
tions between the workman and the capitalist,
If the first is, not placed in a condition to bear
competition with the latter. And that this
may become possible, it is before all things
21E43048aq to emancipate him from the °dims

and humiliating political tutelage which weighs
upon him, And it is necestery, in. order to
emancipate the politician, to restore to him his
rights- as a man and a citizen; the one and
the other cannot possibly be obtained during
the reign of privilege. It is, besides, a delu.7
sion to hope for a serious and durable amelioral
Lion of the economic conditions of the
working class unless they participate in
public life and cooperate by their votes in
the formation of the laws. ,

Association may compel the capitalist to re-.
munerate labour more liberally and more
equally, but be will return to the system of
tyrannizing over the. operative as soon as
resistance ceases on the part of the latter.
Strikes are an expedient, not an efficient means
of producing the economic amelioration of
,the
working daises, which, .t.iiider present Condi-
tions, cannot hold out in a state Of hostility
With those' who detain the instruments of
labour. The best guarantee for both. the one
and the other is in laws freely voted,, discussed,
and accepted by either party, for laws which
regulate the relations between capitalists Said
operatives cannot be obtained- from those
whose interest it is to prolong the present
disorder in the sphere of politics and .economy,
since it is precisely to that disorder that the
present system owes its reason for existence.
Hence working men's associations, while-seek-
ing instruction in the phenomena of economical
science, and endeavouring to bring about an
immediate improvement in
.the condition of
the Workman,, as a Step towards a more equal
distribution of wealth and labeur,.' should
never lose sight of the fact that the essential
Condition of
,economical ernancipatiOn is the
association of the civil, political, and adminis-
trative rights of popular severeignty, alienated
to the advantage of a microscopic minority.
Those workingnien are deceived
.or 'betrayed
who 'forbid the mention of politics , their
aesemblies. and statutes, giving up the exer-
cise of their civil, and political rights for a
deceptive material advantage.

This advice froa a fereig,a source is, at
least, worthy of attention at the present time,
when the Conservative party has had the wit
to use the tempting bait of " material ad-
vantage," ads evidently ready to offer many
a substantial mess of pottage ha exchange for
the political birthright of the workman. You
shall have nearly all you want, say the Con-
servative magnates, provided you leave it to
us how, and when you bhali. get it... Bocial
reforms thus obtained, one by one, .from the
tardy justice of a privileged, class, are
surely but makeshifts, compared to the. ex-
pedient of once for all scouring the command
of the political machinery necessary for
carrying them out as soon as they are
wanted.

articles.title: TEE WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
TEE WEEK'S NEWS.

Mr. Morley, M.P., presided over the fourth
annual taeeting of the Tottenham Deaconesses'
Institution, which was held, on Saturday after-
noon. The amount of the progress of the
organization was of a satisfactory nature, and
it was stated that amongst the correspondence
of the year testifying to the benefits resulting
from the efforts of the nurses during the late
war was a letter from' the Empress of Ger-
many. Several donatiohs were announced,
including an additional one of £5OO from the
chairman, and a similar amount from Mr. John
Morley.

The first meeting of the Coaching Club took
place in Hyde-park on Saturday. There were
21 drags, and the 84 horses were described as
having been in splendid eondition.

On Sunday the Birmingham and Worcester
Canal burst its banks in the neighbourhood
of Edgbaston. The damage to property is
considerable, but there has been no loss of
life.

A second meeting of the E ympathisers with
the claimant to the Tichborne baronetcy was
held at Bristol on Saturday evening. Reso-
lutions in acoordance with the object of the
gathering were carried with much enthusiasm.
Mr. Guildford Onslow, M.P., and the Claimant
were among the speakers.

A correspondent sends an account of three
military executions which took place at Ver-
sailles on Saturday morning. Two of the
prisoners had been convicted on the charge of
being concerned in the massacre of the
Dominicans just a year ago. The other was
accused of causing the death of a chemist who
refused to assist in making a barricade during
the final struggle of the Commune. All three
prisoners shouted Vire is Commune! as the
firing party levelled their rifles. The scene
wkict took place when the bodies were placed
in the rough boxes used as coffins was both
disgusting and horrible.

A cable telegram from Now York announces
that, after eight hours' secret debate, the
American Senate has recommended that the
Supplementary Article to the Washington
Treaty should. be ratified. The motiou was
carried by 42 votes against 9, twenty members
abstaining from voting. During the debate
strong opposition was manifested, and much
annoyance is expressed at the result. The
New York World and Herald both write in
severe terms against the decision arrived at
by the Senate.

A debtor having agreed to pay ss. in the
pound in two sums, one of the creditors, on
the second instalment not being forthcoming,
brought an action for the original debt. Mr.
Registrar Elpring.Riee, following the dictum of
the Chief judge, has, however, held that a
creditor, by assenting to take a composition,
barred himself from further remedy, and
could only enforce the terms of the liquidation.
He therefore continued an interim injunction,
which had been obtained, to restrain the action.

The Priuoe and Priuoess of Wales continue
to remain in Paris. They have visited the
Exhibition of Pictures in the Champs Elysees,
and on Friday night the Prince went to the
theatre. The Princess was, however, too much
fatigued by her rapid journey from Switzer-
land to accompany him.

A. letter from Bayreuth describes the cere-
monies which have taken place there in con-
nection with the proposed theatre which is to
be erected in honour of Herr Wagner, the
composer. As already announced, the festival
out of doors was interfered with by bad wea-
ther, but the proceedings which took place in
the Opera House, and the musical perform-
ances, excited great enthusiasm. On the pre-
vious day—his birthday--llerr Wagner re-
ceived a highly flattering message by tele-
graph from the King of Bavaria.

The death is announced of the Hon. Philip
Pleydell-Bouverie, son of the second Earl of
Radnor, at Clyffe-hall, near Devizes, on the
23rd inst. Debrett's Peerage states that the
deceased gentleman was born 1788; sat as
M.P. for Cockermouth 1830-1, for Downton
1831-2, and for Berkshire 1857-05; was a
Deputy-Lieutenant and a J.P. for Somerset-
shire, of which county ho was High Sheriff
1843; and married, 1811, Maria who died
1862), sister of the first 13aron Heytesbury, by
whom ho had issue.

Sunday, being Trinity Sunday, according to
annual custom, the Judges went in state to
St. Paul's Cathedral, for the purpose of under-
going the ceremony of churching. They were
met at the cathedral by the Lord Mayor, Sir
O. 3. Gibbons, Sir John Bennett, the Under
Sheriffs, the Chamberlain, the Recorder, the
Common Serjeant, the Town Clerk, &a. The
sacred edifice was more crowded than haa
been known for Nula time at a similar
ceremony.

A Cabinet Council was held on Monday,
which was attended by 12 out of the 15
Ministers. Lord Ripon, Lord Halifax, and
the Duke of Argyll were not present.

On Monday the Duke of Edinburgh was re-
elected Master of the Trinity House, and
Captain Sir P. Arrow Deputy Master. ,

When the Corporation of Dublin met to
consider the draft of an address to the Duke
of Edinburgh on his approaching visit to the
Irish capital, Sir J. Gray, M.P., suggested the
embodiment of a hope that before long her
Majesty would come to Dublin to open a
native Parliament, and an expression of opinion
that the time had arrived when political
offenders should not be detained in prison. It
was, however, intimated to the member for
Kilkenny City that persistence in his ideas
would endanger the adoption of any address,
and the draft of the prepared document was
then approved of.

The Hon. E. Lyulph Stanley will be the
Liberal candidate for the representation of
Oldham. He is a son of the late Lord Stanley
of Alderley, who was for some years in Lord
Palmerston's Cabinet as Postmaster-General,
and is 33 years of age. Mr. Stanley was
called to the bar at the Inner Temple in 1865.

At length the Galway election inquiry is at
an end. Judge Keogh has unseated Captain
Nolan, on the ground that there had been un-
due influence on the part of the Roman
Catholic clergy, many of whom had been
guilty of conduct which he strongly con-
demned.

The French Derby a Chantilly, on Sunday,
was won by Revigny, the favourite. The
weather was splendid, and the attendance
very large.

Sir Henry Rawlinson, President of the Royal
Geographical Sooiety, took the chair at the
annual meeting, which was held on Monday.
A considerable portion of Sir Henry's address
was occupied in a narrative of the circum-
stances whioh had led to the sending out of the
Livingstone Search expedition, towards whioh
upwards of £5,000 had been subscribed, A.
letter from Lieutenant Dawson, the com-
mander of the Expedition, dated April 9, was
read. Up to that time there had been no com-
munication with either Dr. Livingstone or Mr.
Stanley, the Special Commissioner of the
New York Herald.

An interpleader issue in the Court of Com-
mon Pleas raised an interesting question
affecting the right of married women to their
earnings. Mrs. Digges, a dancer at the Hay-
market Theatre, had lived apart from her
husband since 1868; and had maintained her-
self. Some goods in her apartments having
been seized upon an execution against her
husband, the present issue was to determine to
whom they belonged. The actress contended
that by the statute of 1870 the property was
hers, it having been bought with money
earned by a married woman when living apart
from her husband. A formal verdict was taken
for the plaintiff, subject to the opinion of
the full court upon the question of law.
In the case of " Digges V.--Gadderer," in
which an actress at the Haymarket raised the
question whether the earnings of a wife living
apart from her husband could be seized for
the payment of his debts, the Court of Com-
mon Pleas on Wednesday granted a rule which
will bring the matter before the Judges for
their decision.

It is the practice of some eabmen, upon meet-
ing with a band of volunteers out for a march,
to break the ranks, and there have been in-
stances in which injury has resulted. One of
these offenders on Monday came before the
Marylebone Police-onurt, and be was fined
two guineas, including costs.

A man who bad insulted a respectable
married woman, and then kieked her because
she called for assistance, was on Monday sen
termed by the Wandsworth pollee magistrate
to seven days' imprisonment with hard labour.

The disappearance of a traveller to a pub-
lishing house in Paternoster-row, was on Mou-
day mentioned to the Lambeth police magis-
trate by the missing man's wife, who said her
husband had not been hoard of since the 2nd
instant.

At Bow-street, on 'Monday, Mr. Herbert
Crellin, comedian, who was lately summoned
for annoying Mr. Bateman' of the Lyceum
Theatre, made an apology, which was
accepted, and the prosecution was withdrawn.

A commission agent in the City, named
Ash, lately failed for more than .24,000, and
returned his assets as nil." Ills creditors con-
sented to a liquidation, and granted him his
discharge. Mr. Registrar Keene declined to
recognise the proceedings, on the ground that
no estate had been disclosed, An appeal was
made to Mr. Registrar Roche, sitting as Chief
Judge, who .bass hOvevoi'l caluned, the de-
cision.

Lord Northbrook left Bombay for Calcutta
on the 30th April, and reached the latter
place 'on the 3rd instant. During his stay in
Bombay he presided at the unveiling of the
statue of the Queen presented to the city by
the Guieowar of Baroda. At this his first
public appearance in India his lordship seems
to have made a very favourable impression.
The Bombay Gazette says that he performed
his task with so much genuine good feeling
and hearty interest in, and admiration of,
Bombay, that he won from his audience a
more cordial greeting than it ever before heard
given there to a Governor or Governor-Gene-
ral. The gift of the statue was intended to
commemorate the assumption by the Queen of
the direct government of India.

In Westminster Abbey on Tuesday, a ser-
mon was preached by the Bishop of Derry, in
connection with the annual service of the
Bishop of London Fund, and to its purposes
the offertory was devoted.

It is announced in the Gazette, that General
Sir T. C. Van Straubenzee has been appointed
Governor of Malta' and Mr. Anthony Mus-
grave, Governor of Natal.

From April Ist to the 25th instant the Ex-
chequer receipts amounted to £10,432,436, as
compared with £9,712,312 in tbe corresponding
period of last year. The expenditure has been
£10,849,909. On Saturday last the balance
in the Bank of England was £6,950,044.

It is said that Lieutenant-General Sir Sid-
ney Cotton, K.C.8., Colonel of the 10th Foot,
has been offered and accepted the vacant
position of Governor of Chelsea Hospital.

Aidlle. Emilie von der Meersch has returned
to England with her famous performing birds.
These latter have now acquired an European
reputation, and have been presented to almost
every crowned head in Europe. Mdlle. von
der Mcerseh does not at present intend to give
any public performances, but will confine her-
self to attending private parties.

William Henry Whiting, a carter's lad,
about sixteen years of age, has been committed
by the Hampshire coroner for trial on a charge
of wilfully murdering Gorge Worthington,
aged twenty, by stabbing him on the high
road at Itohen Abbas, on Saturday last. It
appears that the two had quarrelled'over their
teams when Worthington struek Whiting,
and die latter drew his knife and stabbed him
in the ohest, causing instantaneous death.

The proseoution against a Mrs. Howard,
which has been repeatedly before the Maryle-
bone police magistrate on a charge of having
stolen two rings, the property of the Hon.
Maria Bingham, has collapsed, and the defend-
ant discharged.

The Crown Prince and Princess of Italy
arrived in Berlin on Tuesday. They were
received at the railway station by the Emperor,
the Prince Imperial of Germany, and Prince
Frederick Charles, and conducted to the
Palace.

A special telegram from Bayonne announces
that a proclamation issued by Marshal Serrano,
granting the insurgents a delay of three days
in which to accept the amnesty, has caused
much popular annoyance at Bilbao, it being
regarded as an act of misplaced leniency.

At the Mansion-house, Sir R. M. Stephen-
son and Mr. G. W. 'Brown, the chairman and
secretary of the Smyrna and Aidin line of the
Ottoman Railway, has been charged with
having unlawfully conspired to obtain a quota-
tion of the shares upon the Stock Exchange.
The prosecutor is a Mr. Pickering, and his
complaint is, that the quotation of the shares
was managed in contravention of the rules of
the Stock Exchange, which require that two-
thirds of the capital of a company shall first
be subscribed for by the public, and the deposit
paid upon them. After the examination of one
or two witnesses, the inquiry was adjourned
until Friday, the defendants being released on
their own recognizances.

It was recently stated by a Paris paper
--
the Evenement—that according to rumours in
circulation, Marshal Benin° was only sub-
jected, to a sort of fictitious detention at Ver-
sailles, being at liberty to go out whenever he
pleased. Tuesday's Journet (Violet declares
that this information is quite incorrect. A
Paris correspondent says that the foundation
for the story probably was, that Marshal Bazaine
gees out every day to a little house outside
his garden, which has been taken bg General
de itiviere for the purpose of examining the
prisoner and preparing the indictment.

la a ease heard at Worshis
it
on Tues-
day, a constable explained that t was a part
of the instructions of the police to take a
person into custody who refused to move on
when requeste& to do so. The magistrate
inquired
.whether this would apply if the
disobedient one was sober, and, was informed
by the policeman that such a can would be of
an exceptional nature.

The increasingly prevalent offence of
threatening a witness was the subject of
inquiry at Marylebone Police-court, when a
woman named Gribble, 27 years of age, was
sent to prison, in default of finding two
sureties of £2O each to keep the peace tor ail
months.

A correspondent says, in reference to
the weather in New York, that after
a prolonged and remarkably inclement season,
which, in addition to a fair allowance of
rain, snow, frost, and other pleasant features
of winter, had also the merit of possessipg
more than feminine fickleness, the most in-
tense summer heat has come upon us without
a note of warning, and the thermometer has
suddenly jumped into the nineties. The last
few days seem to have taken New Yorkers by
surprise. Even sunstrokes may now be looked
for, as such heat has not been known at ails
season for many years in this city. The indi-
cations are that we shall have a summer of
unwonted heat, and that those who remain in
the city may expect a taste of more than
tropical fierceness during the dog days.

An application was made on Saturday to the
Court of Common Pleas for a rule to set aside
the nonsuit in the action lately brought a n
gai_st
the proprietor of a music-hall In the Cam-
bridge-heath-road, to recover a penalty of 1:100
for having permitted dancing in his place of
entertainment. The Court, however, refused
to interfere, on the ground that the person who
instituted the proceedings was a common
informer, and not a "party grieved," within
the meaning of the statute.

It appears that the great storm at Madras,
of which we have received full particulars by
the Overland Mail, was the most fearful that
has been known there for forty years. A large
number of vessels were in the roads; but only
three of them escaped. Nine European ships
and seventeen native craft were driven ashore
and became complete wrecks. The pier,
moreover, was broken in two, as in 1868. On
land, also, a good deal of damage was done—
trees being blown down, houses unroofed, and
some lives lost. The city itself, .says the
Madras Mail, has not presented such a scene
of desolation since the great cyclone in 1865.
The river and the islands were flooded, and
some of the principal thoroughfares were
almost impassable, owing to the number of
trees and branches of trees blown down. The
Madras Athenceum considers that the cala-
mity must impress every one with the necessity
of securing the safety of vessels in the roads'
by the construction of a harbour or break-
water.

In an account of the great fire at Yeddo on
the 3rd April, it is stated by the Japan Mail
that 50,000 persons have been rendered home-
less by the calamity. It is estimated that from
250 to 300 perished, and thatthe damage done
must exceed a couple of millions of dollars. A.
gale was raging at the time, which carried the
sparks far and wide, and caused the fire to
spread with marvellous rapidity. Two square
miles of the city were laid. waste, and 10,000
houses destroyed. The misery of the people
who have been burnt out, and who are com-
pelled to camp in the open air, is described as
terrible to witness.

A New York telegram announoes that tuur
steamers and nearly forty sailiPg vessels
engaged in the sea fishing trade on the coast of
Labrador and Newfoundland have been wrecked
among the ice, and that all hands have
perished.

Three men were on Tuesday charged at
Bow-street with having carried on betting
transaotions in a house in Broad-street,
Bloomsbury. One of them was fined X5O,
and the others were discharged.

A cab-driver has been convicted at Wands-
worth Police-court of having used abusive
language and left his vehicle unattended. Tic
was fiued £2 Os., with the alternative a tlYe
week? imprisonment.

Some consideration may well be riven to the
suggestion that has been, made respecting the
location of Newgate Prison and the adjacent
buildings. There is no doubt that the entire
neighbourhood suffers from the gloom and dis-
credit inseparable from the gaol and its
surroundings; and if the removal of these into
some less conspicuous spot could be miaow.
plished, a very acceptable relief would thereby
be acoorded to the district. There are other

articles.title: ESSAYS FOR THE PEOPLE.
articles.text:
ESSAYS FOR THE PEOPLE.

POVERTY.

When we look around many parts of
London, and especially such parts as White-
chapel, Bethnal-green, Poplar, and other
localities almost too numerous to mention, the
poverty-stricken condition of many of the
people residing in those parts is truly heart-
rending. Vast numbers of them, when they
rise at mailing, know not how or where to
obtain a breakfast. It is also an ac-
knowledged truth' that there are thousands
of men, who have to feed and house
themselves with sums ranging from five to
fifteen shillings per week. A great many
readers may think this is an overdrawn state-
ment (especially if they are not in any manner
conversant with the ways and means of the
lower orders of society.) TO those who do
happen to think that it is so, I simply say,
investigate this question for yourselves; go and
enquire at the many common lodging-houses,
existing in various parts of London and
suburbs and most large towns, there you will
see poverty in the extreme, there you will see
men herded together like so many cattle, iii
dingy dark thoroughfares, abounding with
squator and dirt. And yet there are men
doomed to live in such places, through bodily in-
firmities and other unavoidable causes, with an
idea of the beautiful, and in some eases well-
educated; to such men it must be hateful
almost to live. True, on the other hand, a
greater portion of the inhabitants of such
places have, no idea of a better state of living,
and appear perfectly' satisfied with their lot,
but, still it is detrimental to the interests of
society for all that. Again, there are thousands
of working men and small-householders, that
can hardly manage to pay their rent and keep
up a decent appearance, living on the com-
monest of. food, their children half-fed, half-
clothed, and half-educated, and when old age
comes upon them and their health fails them,
they fall a burden on the resources of their
grown up sons and daughters, who are mostly
poor themselves, or else, the alternative of
going into the workhouse. What a prospect '
for a man! who has expended the best portion
of his days in honest hard labour to keep him-
self and family a little respectable; the grim
walls of a workhouse, almost equal to a prison,
and yet he is told " To rest and be thankful"
by the very class of men that should be help-
ing him out of his difficulty, and bringing his
mind to a fit state, to receive the blessings of
Christianity. I fearlessly avow, for my
part, that such a state of things is brought
about by the. selfish nature of man himself,
and that it is not "all for the best," for God,
1 am sure, never intended that the poverty
now existing should be so. Picture to your
mind the state of a Mall'S feelings; he is think-
ing of his hard lot, he sees his sons as bad off
as he is himself, and unable to help. him in
his old age, when .he needs it most. Such a
man's mind must be in a truly pitiable state.
GEORGE EDWARD TYLEY.

articles.title: CHAPTER I.—lts CAUSES.
articles.text:
CHAPTER I.—lts CAUSES.

It will be necessary in this chapter to trace
the causes of poverty to its primitive bearing.
Now there are many causes to which poverty
may be attributed, such as intemperance, a
want of prudence and economy, depression of
trade, or deuness of provisions, etc., but
which may be classed as mere secondary
causes, when we compare them with what may
be considered as one of the main causes, viz., the
hereditary system of disposing of land and
other properties, a system that is very pre-
valent among the upper classes of society at the
present day, that is of leaving the bulk of their
property to their eldest descendant. Moreover
this is a system which can not, and never ought to
be, received as a true one by any thinking man.
For supposing this system to be right, and in
just accordance with the laws of nature, then
I say your lords and your dukes, or by :whatever
title they may be known, hold their estates
and other properties unlawfully, because the
earth and everything upon it would at the
present time belong to one man alone by lineal
descent from Adam, whom God created at the
commencement of the world, and whom we
recognise as being the first man placed thereon.
Therefore it is absurd and inconsistent with
all human belief to think for a moment that
the hereditary system can possibly be right.
I consider it, for my own part, the duty of a
father, if he has six children, to share his
property equally amongst them, and their
right also to the same; and if he should leave
it all to one, it is in point of fact a decided
robbery, for the others being born of the same
parents, although at different times, yet have
the same claim for their sympathy and love as
the first one has, consequently should have the
same claim in reference to their (the parent's)
property. And had, at the first onset, mankind
been placably disposed, and have acted fair
i and upright n their dealings towards their
respective descendants, and left them that
which was due to them, poverty would never
have been known, men would have traded
with each other in a reciprocal manner, and
wars and rumours of wars would never have
been heard of. But man being selfish and
greedy by nature, gave every facility for
another great cause of poverty, he not being

13

satisfied with that which was aufllcitmt for hie
sustenance, devised a method whereby he
might utilize the value- -of what might other.
wise rot—viz., by the use of coin, which
being unperishable, he might exchange the
perishable for the unpenshable, thereby
as Locke has it, making it his right by
the use of money what otherwise would
not be his right in substance, there being
more than he would require for his use.
This more particularly applies to wheat, fruit
&c.; hut the same argument may be applied
to the los3ession of lands and so on.

THE PEOPLE'S GSRDENS, WILLESDEN.

The opening of these pleasant gardens for
the season took place on Saturday, when about
.500 persons, all members tif the People's
Garden Club, or visitors specially invited,
were present, and passed a very enjoyable day
and evening. These gardens, the property of
an association of working men, known as the
People's Garden Company, are about 60 acres
in extent, situated on Old Oak common, about
five minutes' walk from Willesden Junction
Station. The gardens have been much im-
proved since the experimental season of last
year, and are now laid out with flower beds,
terraces, and ,gravelled walks. There are also
cricket-grounds and croquet lawns; the latter
were largely patronised by the ladies. Re-
freshment pavilions have been erected in variou-
parts of the gardens, besides a large banquets
ting-hall, capable of dining from 800 to
1,000 persons, and which is also used as a tea-
room. Swings, a gymnasium, and steam-
roundabouts have also been fitted up for
the use of the juveniles and visitors. A theatre,
concert and lecture hall, is in course of erection,
but will not be completed in time for use during
the present season. The leading feature of the
gardens; however, at present is its splendid
dancing platform, with a commodious orchestra
in the centre, erected at a cost of about
£l,OOO. This platform is said to be the largest
dancing platform in Europe, and is one-
eighth of a mile in circumference. In addi-
tion to the dancing on Saturday, the company's
band being in attendance during the day, the
platform was utilised at intervals for bicycle
races, on machines made expressly for the
gardens, and these races afforded much satis.
faction and amusement to the spectators. Thera
were also some excellent part and chorus
singing in the open air, by the ladies and
gentlemen forming the choir of the company.
The entertainments were brought to a close at
ten o'clock, the company. returning to town by
the 10.30 train from 'Willesden Junction. The
gardens are under the management of Mr.
Henry Bolleter, of the German Club, Foley.
street, a gentleman who has had much ex-
perience in the management of similar
gardens on the Continent. The gardens will
remain open every day, Sunday included, up
to the end of September. There is no money.
taken at the doors, and admission can only be
obtained by persons becoming members of the
People's Garden Club, by taking a ss. season
ticket, or by friends of members receiving a
special ticket of invitation.

THE BALLOT BILL.

The Bill of the Session—the Parliamentary
and Municipal Elections Bill—has been re-
printed to show its condition after its handling
by the Rouse of Commons in Committee. The
first thing - that will strike any one who takes
up thifs Bill is that the longest part of it con-
sists of schedules. No less than 65 rules, or
laws, for elections are placed in a schedule.,
which is declared to be "part of the Bill,"
The Bill peeper contains a more outline of the
mode of procedure at elections; and the details
are in the schedules. It is possible that some
inconvenience inay arise from this method.
The 13i11 has grown longer by discussion; and
the 43 folio pages laid before the House have
increased to SO new. It would be tedious to
repeat the story of the proceedings to he taken
at, elections by ballot, but alterations made in
the Bill deserve notice. The Bill proper
oentipies 15 pages. It provides now that at an
uncontested election the returning officer IS to
declare the result, not at the expiration of the
time appointed for the election, but at the ex-
piration of one hour after that time; objection
may be made to a nominatio4 paper within
the hour. The withdrawal of a candidate,
which must be during the time appointed for
the election, may be done by his proposer if
the candidate is out of the United Kingdom.
The clause directing that after the close of the
poll the ballot-boxes shall be sealed up, adds,
—" so as to prevent the introduction of addi-
tional ballot-papers." To the clanse enjoining
secresy on the clerks and agents in attendance
at the pollina•-station in added :--" No
person shall directly or indirectly induce
any voter to display his ballot-paper after he
shall have marked the same, so as to make
known to any
.person the name of the eandi-
date for or against whom he has so marked his
vote." The penalty is iinprisonment not ex-
ceeding six months. in the clauses relating
to Ireland it is provided that the 6th section of
the Bill, allowing the use (free of charge), for
taking the poll; of a room in a school receiving
aid from the Parliamentary. grant, is not to
apply to any school tieljouung or adjacent to
any church or other place of worship, nor to
any ctiool connected with a nunnery or other
religious establishment. Clauses have been
introduced into the Bill; providing for the
punishment of personation, and the correction
of the poll on a scrutiny in respect of votes
obtained by personation, bribery, treating, Or
undue influence. The clauses haVe been
transferred to the 'Ballot Bill from its com-
panion the Corrupt ' Practices Bill. The
offence of personation, or aiding ia it, ie made
felony; and it is to be the duty of the return-
ing officer to prosecute any person whom he
may believe guilty of it. A candidate found guilty
of it, by himself or his agents, on the trial of an
eleetion petition, will be incapable of sitting for
that constituency during the Parliament then
in existence, The "Rules for Elekions "
have been somewhat altered in committee.
